Oil: Japan to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill reserves drained by the Hormuz crisis, and triples the storage offered to Riyadh

Japan announced on 20 November that it intends to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to rebuild its strategic reserves, which were drawn down during the war between the United States and Iran. Tokyo is also lending Riyadh an additional 16 million barrels of storage, for a total of around 24 million [1][4][5].
According to a joint statement published by Japan's Ministry of Economy (METI), Japan plans to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi oil for its national stockpiles [3][5].
The purchase remains conditional: it depends on “favourable market conditions” and on the completion of Japanese internal procedures [1][2].

Japan will temporarily make 16 million barrels of storage capacity in its national depots available to Saudi Arabia. Riyadh already had around 8 million: the total will reach around 24 million barrels [4][5].
Saudi Arabia has already begun refilling its tanks in Japan, according to the statement [1][3].
The arrangement has existed since 2010: in exchange for the storage, Japan gets a priority right to buy this oil in an emergency [1][2].
Japan is among the importers that tapped their emergency reserves when the war between the United States and Iran disrupted passage through the Strait of Hormuz [1][2].
In September, Japanese refiners said they had enough crude until the end of November thanks to released state stocks, but considered the situation uncertain from December onwards [7].

The key takeaway: Japan is rebuilding its “oil insurance” now, before winter, while the threat to Hormuz has not gone away. By pledging to buy only if prices are favourable, Tokyo keeps control over filling its tanks at the best moment [1][2][7].

Japan depends almost entirely on the Gulf: its refiners get around 95% of their crude from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar, and around 70% of that oil passes through Hormuz, according to Rigzone [6].

For Saudi Arabia, storage in Japan is a commercial asset: its oil is already on site, a few days from Asian refineries, instead of having to cross a war zone. In September, Riyadh was already bypassing the strait by transferring crude from ship to ship outside Hormuz [7][10].

The move contrasts with the United States, whose strategic reserve is at its lowest since 1982, according to Energy News Beat [9]. Purchases to refill reserves add demand, which can support crude prices when they fall.

Strategic reserves are state stockpiles used when oil stops arriving. When a large country like Japan refills them, it adds demand to the market, and that can slow the drop in pump prices you are hoping for, in Europe too.

How it works: strategic oil reserves

Major importers keep state stockpiles to last several weeks if deliveries stop. In the middle of a crisis, they sell some to refineries, which calms prices. Once the crisis is over, they have to be refilled by buying on the market: that is what Japan is doing [1][2]. Storage for a producing country, such as Saudi Arabia, is a variant: Riyadh rents tanks in Japan, places its oil there to sell to Asian refiners, and Tokyo can buy it first in an emergency [1][4]. Japan is buying “if market conditions are favourable” [1]: it fills its tanks when prices fall, which can cushion declines.

Anthropic brushes its IPO price in only its second session: 5 cents from $83, the biggest stock market debut in history wobbles

On Friday 20 November, in its second session on the Nasdaq, Anthropic stock fell 9.13% to $88.30, after dropping to $83.05, 5 cents from its IPO price. The banks nonetheless exercised their full over-allotment option, bringing the amount raised to $93.5 billion [2].
Anthropic stock (ticker ANT) closed on Friday at $88.30, down 9.13%, in its second session on the Nasdaq [2]. It was already down 9.6% before the open, according to 24/7 Wall St. [1].
At its low, it fell to $83.05, just 5 cents above the $83 price paid by investors in the IPO [2].

The day before, on its first day, the stock had opened at $111.50, climbed as high as $115.10, then finished at $97.17 (+17.1%) [2]. In two sessions, it has therefore lost more than 20% from its peak.
The banks exercised their over-allotment option (the “greenshoe”) in full, bringing the amount raised to around $93.5 billion [2].

The fall came on the day the S&P 500 lost 3.70% to 6,910.42 points and the Dow Jones 1.93% to 48,147.33 points. Several media outlets linked Wall Street's slide into correction to this debut, seen as disappointing [6].
A strategist quoted by Yahoo Finance warns against the temptation to “chase the IPO” [3]. The group of major banks in charge of the offering is under pressure to defend the price [4].
Next milestone: around 300 million shares can be sold from 15 December, which could weigh on the share price [2][3].

The key takeaway: the IPO price, $83, has become the line the whole market is watching. If it is breached, investors who bought in the offering would lose money [2][4]. The stock even fell as much as 15% below the previous day's level during the session [5].

Anthropic was supposed to prove that AI is worth the sums invested. A stock that falls back towards its starting price in two days sends the opposite signal, and that doubt spread across the whole tech sector on Friday [3][6].

The banks that organised the offering have a tool to support the share price: the over-allotment option, which allows them to buy back shares on the market if the price threatens to fall below $83. The fact that they exercised it in full means they sold all the planned additional shares [2][4].
On 15 December, employees and early investors will be able to sell part of their shares. This is the end of the “lock-up period”, often a tricky moment for newly listed companies [2].

If you bought Anthropic shares in the IPO, your Thursday gain almost vanished in a single day. A heavily publicised stock market debut is no guarantee of gains: the first two weeks are often the most volatile.

How it works: the “greenshoe”, the safety net of IPOs

In an IPO, banks generally sell slightly more shares than planned; this is the over-allotment. If the share price rises, the company issues these additional shares and collects more money (this is what brought Anthropic's raise to $93.5 billion [2]). If the price falls below the IPO price, the banks can instead buy these shares back on the market, which supports the price. This safety net mainly applies during the first few weeks. On 15 December, the end of the lock-up period will open another stage: around 300 million shares can be sold [2][3].

COP31: after two days of overtime, the Turkish presidency says it has a deal, but the word “fossil” still divides

Overnight from Saturday to Sunday in Antalya, the Turkish president of COP31, Murat Kurum, presented a text that “all parties can accept”. The negotiations ran two days past the 20 November deadline, stuck on fossil fuels and money for climate adaptation [1][2][3].

Delegations had until 3am GMT on Sunday to object to the text, ahead of an adoption session scheduled for 6am GMT [1][2]. Murat Kurum says concerns about fossil fuels and adaptation finance have been taken into account [1].

The first draft, published on 16 November by Australia, co-chair of the negotiations, called for “accelerating” the transition away from fossil fuels and for tripling adaptation aid to developing countries to reach at least $120 billion a year by 2035 [9].

The version of Thursday 19 November removed any mention of fossil fuels from its 80 articles [5]. It keeps the idea of tripling adaptation aid by 2035, but without a dollar figure or baseline year; a UN committee is to propose a calculation method [5][12].
The text retains the Turkish target known as “35 by 35”: raising electricity to 35% of global final energy consumption by 2035, a voluntary goal [6].

Who is blocking? Saudi Arabia and its allies in the Arab Group reject any mention of fossil fuels, arguing that each country must decide on its energy alone [7]. On the other side, a dozen countries, from France to the Solomon Islands, are demanding by letter “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”; Panama threatened to walk out [7][8].

According to the UN and The National, around 130 countries want the final text to keep a reference to the transition away from fossil fuels [5][10]. The European Union warned that the COP risked becoming a “fossil fuel summit” [7].
On Saturday, the EU and Saudi Arabia were brought together for a compromise [8]. The United States did not send a delegation, nor did Israel and Myanmar [11].
The key takeaway: COP31 comes down to one sentence. Either the text says the world must move away from oil, gas and coal, or it stays silent and producers keep a free hand [7][4].

For the economy, two issues matter. First, money: poor countries want a figure for adapting (dykes, resilient crops). Without a figure or starting point, the promise to “triple” is hard to verify [12].
Second, energy: the “35 by 35” target pushes for electrifying transport, heating and industry, which will require investment in grids. But its inclusion in the negotiated text is divisive [6].

“There is no possible compromise on science,” said the Danish climate minister [11]. Australia's Chris Bowen had warned that the first drafts were “not the final version” [6]. If no agreement is reached, the conference will end without a decision and resume next year [8].

Nothing changes right away when you fill up your tank. But it steers public and private money for years: more electricity, stronger grids, perhaps fewer oil projects. The signal to watch for: does the word “fossil” come back in the adopted version?

“We are worried”: Taiwan warns Mark Carney's Canada against dependence on China, three days after the Shenzhen summit

On Saturday 21 November, at the Halifax International Security Forum, Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi warned that by moving closer to China, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was exposing himself to the “economic coercion” he himself denounces. Taiwan also accuses Beijing of exploiting the photo from the Shenzhen summit [1][2].
Chen Ming-chi, Taiwan's Deputy Foreign Minister, spoke to the AP news agency on the sidelines of the Halifax International Security Forum in Canada on Saturday 21 November [1][3].
His message comes down to three words: “We are worried.” Taiwan has learned from experience that depending on Beijing comes at a cost, he explained [1].
He noted that Taiwan sharply reduced its economic dependence on China after Beijing used trade restrictions to put pressure on the island [2].
He warned against Chinese electric cars: they could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks, even if they were made in Canada [2][3].
Mark Carney has nonetheless said that Canada could turn to Chinese manufacturers if negotiations with Washington fail to protect a viable Canadian auto industry [2].

Chen Ming-chi also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photo from the Shenzhen summit [3], where Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met on Thursday 19 November at the Kylin villa, a first three-way meeting [5].
The deputy minister did, however, welcome Mark Carney's commitment to sign a long-awaited trade cooperation agreement with Taiwan [2][4].

The key takeaway: Taiwan, which Beijing considers part of its territory, is trying to convince “middle powers” such as Canada not to replace their dependence on the United States with a dependence on China.

The paradox is at the heart of Taiwan's message. Mark Carney repeatedly says that great powers are weaponising economic integration, citing US tariffs and Chinese restrictions on critical minerals, and he calls on middle powers to diversify their partners [1]. The deputy minister in fact praised his Davos speech [2].

But for Ottawa, the trade relationship with China is not the same as the far more complicated one between Washington and Beijing [1]. Chen Ming-chi, by contrast, asks whether it is wise to tighten ties with countries that do not share Canada's democratic values [2].

The question of the Shenzhen photo also matters: the image of the three leaders side by side is set to remain the record of the first meeting of its kind between China, Russia and the United States [5]. By accusing Beijing of exploiting it, Taiwan shows that it fears how China uses this image with countries tempted to move closer to it [3].

The question facing Canada also faces Europe: should you buy cheaper Chinese cars and technology, at the risk of depending on Beijing if relations sour? What Taiwan is saying is that a single supplier can one day turn off the tap to apply pressure. Remember that the choice between low prices and security of supply is coming up in every trade debate this year-end.

Ecuador: televised debates this Sunday in Quito and Guayaquil, a week before local elections in which 13.8 million voters will judge Noboa's camp

On Sunday 22 November, the candidates for mayor of Quito and Guayaquil face off on television. On 29 November, 13.8 million Ecuadorians are due to elect 23 prefects, 222 mayors and thousands of local officials, in a vote brought forward by two and a half months and seen as a test for President Daniel Noboa [1][2][5].
The National Electoral Council (CNE) has registered 13,827,643 voters, including 496,308 abroad [1]. Voting is optional from 16 to 18 and over 65 [1].

Voters must elect 23 prefects, 222 mayors, 909 urban and 457 rural municipal councillors, 4,131 members of rural parish councils and seven members of the Citizen Participation Council [1]. In total, 51,731 candidacies have been approved [3].

On 27 March, the CNE voted four to one to bring the election, scheduled for 14 February 2027, forward to 29 November 2026 [5][6]. The campaign runs until 26 November, followed by three days of electoral silence; polling stations will be open from 7am to 5pm [1].

In Quito, ten candidates are running for mayor, including incumbent Pabel Muñoz, who is seeking re-election, and former mayor Jorge Yunda, who is attempting a comeback [3]. The debate is split into groups: Pabel Muñoz and Harold Burbano, candidate of the president's ADN party, appear in the first, Jorge Yunda in the second [4].
In Guayaquil, former mayor Cynthia Viteri is running under the ADN banner (list 7) [7].

Daniel Noboa is not a candidate, but obtained two weeks of leave to campaign, approved by the Assembly on 10 November [8]. On 11 November, he extended the state of emergency in eight provinces by 30 days, for security reasons [9].
The key takeaway: this is the first major vote since Noboa's setback in the November 2025 referendum, and it will show whether his ADN party can gain a foothold in cities and provinces [2][10].

Daniel Noboa was re-elected with 55.63% of the vote in April 2025, but seven months later voters rejected all four of his referendum proposals, including a Constituent Assembly, which was voted down by around 61.6% [10][11].

Quito and Guayaquil matter: city halls manage transport and basic services, and their mayors often become national figures. An ADN victory in these two cities would strengthen the president against the opposition [3][7].
The vote is taking place in a tense security climate, under a state of emergency in eight provinces throughout the campaign [9].
Ecuador sells Europe products you find on the shelves, such as bananas and shrimp. Its political stability and security also matter in the fight against trafficking that passes through its ports.

UN: 9th vote with no winner to succeed Guterres, the organisation risks being left without a leader on 1 January

On Friday 20 November, the Security Council held its ninth straw poll to choose the next UN Secretary-General, without consensus. Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan remains in the lead but is slipping. António Guterres's term ends on 31 December, and the UN is preparing contingency plans, an unprecedented situation [1][2][3].

Rebeca Grynspan (Costa Rica) received 10 “encourage” votes, 4 “discourage” and 1 “no opinion”, according to the tally seen by PassBlue [1]. Of the negative votes, two came from permanent members, which hold a veto [2]. On 5 November, she had 12 favourable votes [2].
Argentina's Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, received 8 favourable and 6 unfavourable votes, including opposition from three permanent members [1][2].
Lana Nusseibeh (United Arab Emirates) received 7 favourable and 6 unfavourable votes, unchanged from the previous poll [1].
Chile's Michelle Bachelet withdrew after the 18 September poll [6].
The race has lasted more than 100 days, the longest succession in UN history according to the Cypriot site Politis [5]. In 2016, it took six rounds to select António Guterres [3].

No Secretary-General has ever left office without a successor [3]. The UN Charter makes no provision for a vacancy: Russian diplomat Kirill Logvinov mentions a short extension for Guterres or a deputy appointed as interim head [3].

The key takeaway: the five permanent members (United States, China, Russia, United Kingdom, France) cannot agree on a name, and each can block a candidate. As long as no one gets through without a veto, the Council cannot recommend a name to the General Assembly [1][3].

Voting is by secret ballot, with three choices: “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion”. According to Reuters, analysts blame this opaque system and the great powers' growing refusal to compromise [3].

Richard Gowan, of the International Crisis Group, believes a vacant post at year-end would be “embarrassing” for the permanent members [3]. Daniel Safran-Hon, a former UN official, notes that without a Secretary-General, “no one would formally be in charge”, even if the Council and the Assembly could continue to meet for a while [3].
The stakes go beyond symbolism: the Secretary-General runs the UN administration. Its officials are already drafting contingency plans in case no one is in charge on 1 January [3][4].

The UN chief governs no country, but carries weight in mediation (Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan) and coordinates humanitarian aid. A UN without a leader means one less voice to calm the crises that move oil or food prices.

Venezuela: 36 military political prisoners on hunger strike for 12 days, denied visits, UN called on for help

At the Ramo Verde military prison near Caracas, dozens of officers held for political reasons have been refusing food since 9 November. On Saturday 21 November, the NGO Clippve denounced the ban on family visits, and relatives are calling for urgent medical care [1][2][3].
The strike began on Monday 9 November with 24 soldiers [4]; the Venezuelan Prison Observatory (OVP) later counted 36 [6].
According to relatives quoted by Infobae, the prison management has restricted their access to water [5].
On Saturday, the Committee for the Release of Political Prisoners (Clippve) denounced the suspension of family visits since the start of the protest [1][2].

Most of the strikers are suffering from weakness and fainting spells, and have reportedly received no care, according to Clippve [2]. Their families are demanding urgent medical attention after eleven days without food [3]. The NGO Justicia, Encuentro y Perdón reports dizziness and disorientation among several of them [7].
The detainees are demanding their release, a review of their cases and the inclusion of military personnel in the ongoing political negotiations [6].
The OVP has asked the UN and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) to take a position; according to the NGOs, the government has not responded to any of these requests [6].
The same day, Clippve called on the families of prisoners and victims to challenge candidacies for the Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), which is being renewed [8].

The key takeaway: the issue of political prisoners, and especially military ones, remains the most sensitive point of Venezuela's transition, and this hunger strike is putting the authorities under pressure [1][6].

The figures diverge: the NGO Foro Penal counts 321 political prisoners, including 140 military personnel, while Delcy Rodríguez's interim government says the amnesty law has benefited nearly 9,000 people [1][6]. The soldiers feel forgotten by this process, hence their demand to be included in the negotiations [6].

The health situation is worrying: after more than a week without food, NGOs describe weakness, dizziness and disorientation, with no medical care according to the families [2][7]. The ban on visits also prevents any outside monitoring of their condition [1][2].
The renewal of the TSJ, the country's highest court, will be another test: it is the court that rules on political and electoral disputes [8].

What happens in Venezuela, an oil country at the heart of regional tensions, matters for energy and for immigration to Europe. But here, the stakes are first and foremost human: the way the authorities treat these detainees will show whether the transition is real.

Tonga: national state of emergency over El Niño drought, water reserved for essentials and power cuts

The Kingdom of Tonga, in the South Pacific, has been under a state of emergency since Thursday 19 November because of a drought linked to the El Niño phenomenon. Acting Prime Minister Viliami Latu has ordered that water be reserved for vital needs until at least 16 December. Fiji had already declared a state of disaster [1][2][5].

The state of emergency covers all of Tonga's land and waters, from 11am on 19 November until 11am on 16 December, unless extended or lifted early [2]. One media outlet gives 17 December as the end date [4]. The government plans a review before the deadline [1].
Government offices, businesses, villages and households must save water and reserve it for drinking, cooking and essential hygiene [4].

Several areas of the main island, Tongatapu, and of the outer islands are already experiencing water cuts, the US embassy reports [6]. The electricity company Tonga Power is resorting to load shedding [7].

The National Disaster Risk Management Office is coordinating aid through a national emergency operations centre and centres on each island [4]. In early November, it was already planning to distribute water with the armed forces [8].
According to Tonga's meteorological service, El Niño is expected to peak in December, with below-normal rainfall until January 2027 and possible effects until June 2027 [3][8].
Tonga has already received five drought insurance payouts in 2026 to fund its response in several island groups [9].
The key takeaway: after Fiji, a second Pacific country has moved into emergency mode because of El Niño, and the drought could last until summer 2027 [3][5].

El Niño is a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean that shifts rainfall zones. For these islands, which depend on rainwater tanks and shallow groundwater, a few months without rain threaten drinking water, crops, livestock and public health [1][8].

The economic impact is heavy: agriculture is suffering, and the electricity company has to ration [7]. The state of emergency, declared under the disaster management law, makes it possible to mobilise public resources and outside aid more quickly [2][3]. “Parametric insurance”, which pays out automatically as soon as a drought threshold is crossed, provides some quick money [9].
The crisis comes during COP31, where Pacific islands are calling for more money to adapt to the climate [10].
What is happening there shows in concrete terms what “adapting to the climate” means: storing water, insuring harvests, keeping the lights on. That is exactly what COP31 is trying to finance.

On Saturday 21 November, an Israeli drone hit a van bringing food to displaced people in Tel al-Hawa, in western Gaza City, killing three men according to the civil defence. When you hear about a “ceasefire” in Gaza, keep in mind that the deaths continue: around 180 in six weeks according to local authorities. The issue of aid, food and tents, remains at the heart of the tragedy for the enclave's inhabitants.

The money has not yet been paid: first comes the opinion of the EU's Economic and Financial Committee, then the Commission's payment decisions. The disbursements are expected by the end of 2026 [3][4].
On a visit to Ilioupoli, in the Athens suburbs, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis welcomed securing “the entirety” of the roughly 36 billion negotiated [2].
The key takeaway: Greece, which only a few years ago emerged from a decade of debt crisis, is receiving every last euro of the EU's post-Covid recovery plan [1][2].

Kyriakos Mitsotakis is using it as a campaign argument ahead of next year's legislative elections: his party, New Democracy, remains clearly ahead in the polls, but without an absolute majority [2]. It remains to be seen how the Greek economy will hold up once this aid ends [6].

These billions come from joint borrowing by the Twenty-Seven, which France is also repaying. The Greek case shows that this plan mainly financed reforms and investment in the most fragile countries of the eurozone.

news.2026-11-22-australie-chine-dialogue: Australia: Albanese returns from an 11-day trip with an AI dialogue with China, days after a tech pact with Washington

Anthony Albanese was due to return to Australia on Saturday 21 November after 11 days abroad. From his visit to China, he brings back the launch of a government-to-government dialogue on artificial intelligence, set out in a joint statement of 20 November [1][2].

The dialogue, provided for in the joint statement of 20 November, will cover the safety, governance and uses of AI [1]. It is the first concrete outcome of Anthony Albanese's meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing [1].
The two countries also pledged to cooperate more on climate, clean energy, health and tourism [1][4].
No timetable, venue or safeguards have been made public for these talks [3].
Anthony Albanese's trip took him to COP31, the ASEAN summit in Manila and APEC in Shenzhen [1].

The key takeaway: Canberra is playing both sides. Australia signed a technology declaration with the United States aimed at protecting the AI supply chain from Chinese interference, and at the same time is opening a dialogue with Beijing on the same subject [1][3].
For Anthony Albanese, the aim is to extend the thaw with China without upsetting Washington, its ally. The actual content of the dialogue remains to be clarified [3].

Like Europe, Australia is trying to talk to everyone on AI without depending on a single camp. Watch what comes of this dialogue: it is a test of the ability of “middle powers” to stay between Beijing and Washington.
